stories.text: John Boot opened a herbalist's shop on Goose Gate in 1849, and his son Jesse was born in the area, into poverty, the next year.[^boots] After John died in 1860 his widow Mary kept the shop going as M & J Boot.[^boots] Jesse became a partner at 21, and in 1883 he built a larger store on the same site, the first of the Boots shops; Nottingham Civic Society put up a plaque here in 2015.[^boots]

74525.sum: Boots on Goose Gate: a bar on Goose Gate. The building dates from about 1805, according to OpenStreetMap. It is Grade II listed as the Lanes and was designed by RC Sutton.

stories.text: The building began in 1839 as a grand Wesleyan chapel on Broad Street. Broadway opened here in 1990, and one of its screens is the only cinema screen designed by Sir Paul Smith.

Hockley has a taste for small cinema. Broadway was the first cinema in the UK to show Quentin Tarantino's Pulp Fiction, and from 2002 to 2011 the district also had The Screen Room, then the smallest commercial cinema in the world.
stories.nm: Pulp Fiction and the Screen Room

74666.sum: Broadway Cinema is an independent cinema and registered charity in Nottingham, England, located in the Hockley area of the city's Creative Quarter. With a mission to inspire creativity and a lifelong love of film, Broadway is one of the UK's leading independent cinemas, attracting circa 200,000 visitors annually to its four-screen cinema, café bar, and creative workspace.

stories.text: Trolleybuses, buses drawing power from overhead wires, first ran on 10 April 1927 and took over the tram routes one by one; the last tram ran in September 1936.[^s1] A depot opened on Parliament Street in June 1929 and is still in use.[^s2] By the end of 1937 the city had 125 trolleybuses, the largest fleet in the country, and at most 157.[^s2] The last ran on 30 June 1966.[^s1]
